claims.text: Controlled thermal annealing that induces uniform nanoscale precipitates in a magnetic high-entropy alloy will increase its coercive field.
The initial magnetic high-entropy alloy can be a single-phase, as-sputtered BCC material.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous elemental distribution and minimal precipitates.
Annealing at an appropriate temperature will induce nanoscale elemental segregation or Cr-V-like precipitate formation.
An annealing regime can induce precipitation while remaining below the threshold for significant grain growth.
The treatment can maintain an overall nanocrystalline grain structure while permitting precipitate nucleation.
Precipitates will nucleate at grain boundaries and triple junctions.
An inert annealing atmosphere will prevent oxidation.
The annealing treatment will produce nanoscale precipitates both at grain boundaries and within grains.
The precipitates will act as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
Precipitate-induced pinning will increase the energy barrier for domain-wall motion.
Increasing the energy barrier for domain-wall motion will increase coercivity.
The annealed sample will have a higher coercive field than a matched as-sputtered untreated sample.
Excessive precipitate coarsening or grain growth may diminish or reverse the coercivity increase.
Analogous precipitate formation has been observed in refractory high-entropy alloys under thermal or irradiation conditions.
TEM can be used to characterize precipitate presence and distribution and grain size in the treated and control samples.
SQUID magnetometry or vibrating-sample magnetometry can determine coercive fields from magnetic hysteresis loops.
